intro: Property managers coordinate tenants, contractors and budgets, which makes general management the natural next step. The closest of the 25 careers below is General and Operations Managers, with a 90% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $105,770, which is 51% more than the $69,990 property managers earn.
why_it_works: Running a building or community means handling repairs, leases, complaints and money, often all on the same day. O*NET rates coordination at 3.75 out of 5 for this job and negotiation at 3.62. Purchasing, administrative and operations management use the same skills. Almost every match needs no extra schooling, and 9 of the top 10 pay more. The gaps are systems analysis and time management.
tips: Purchasing Managers earn $148,080, which is 112% more, and value your vendor negotiations.
Administrative Services Managers earn $114,130, or 63% more, and run facilities much like you do.
Track occupancy, budget and cost savings in numbers; they are the proof management hiring looks for.

faq.q: What jobs can former property managers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are General and Operations Managers (90%), Purchasing Managers (88%) and Financial Managers (84%), based on O*NET 31.0. Administrative Services Managers are also 83% matched and earn $114,130, which is 63% more than the $69,990 property manager median.

faq.q: Which careers for property managers pay more?
faq.a: 18 of the 25 matches pay more than property management. Chief Executives earn $213,990 (206% more), Financial Managers $166,570 (138% more) and Marketing Managers $166,790 (138% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Executive roles usually need a graduate degree or long experience.

faq.q: Do property managers need a degree to move up?
faq.a: Usually not. 24 of the 25 matches need no more education than property managers already have, including all of the top 10. A bachelor's degree is common in close matches, held by 53% of workers in one of them, so results count most.

faq.q: What skills should property managers learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are systems analysis, systems evaluation, time management and instructing. Managing financial resources already rates 3.25 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so analyzing operations and training staff are the main steps toward senior management.
